extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / anatomists / microscopists (readers of the Royal Society)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing short observational/experimental letters or dissection reports for a learned society or scientific journal, emphasizing specimen handling, microscopy, anatomical description, and engagement with prior authorities. Geared to produce reproducible, evidence-based natural history / anatomical reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure for treating a disease
rubrics_metrics.description: In treating of any disease, this author notices, 1. The history of the distemper. 2. The part affected. 3. The causes. 4. The prognostics. 5. The method of cure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this five-part framework to present disease accounts: give a full case history, locate the affected part, discuss causation, offer prognosis, and set out remedies/method of cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed specimen preparation and observational procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly describe how specimens were obtained and handled (e.g. "I took the semen masculum of a dog, which I put into a glass pipe, and wrapped it up in soft leather"), the intervals of observation (e.g. observed 4 days successively; later observed after 7 days), and any manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report container, packing, storage conditions, durations between collection and observation, and any manipulations so readers can judge and reproduce the observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of microscopy and instrument quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear when microscopic observation was decisive (e.g. "when I made use of a very good microscope, I saw ... a very great number of the living animals") and distinguish naked-eye from microscopic findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State instrument quality/usage (at least qualitatively), and note limits of naked-eye inspection versus microscopic observation; demonstrate findings through microscope when claims depend on very small structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat trials and multiple specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Support claims by repeating observations across individuals and species (dogs, bitches, rabbits, sheep) and across multiple timepoints (immediate post-coitus, hours, days, up to several days later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform and report repeated experiments, varying times after mating and using multiple animals, to show consistency and to probe temporal dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative estimation and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide numerical estimates and measurements where possible (e.g. "I found ... not less than 100 millions"; distances like "5 inches and 4-"; sizes compared to sand or a pea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include counts, size comparisons, lengths and relative scales to give quantitative support for qualitative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative engagement with prior authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly cite and address contemporary authorities and contrary opinions (e.g. De Graaf, Harvey, Dr. Grew), and use observations to confirm or rebut their claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss previous literature, explain disagreements, and present direct evidence that supports or contradicts earlier assertions rather than simply asserting superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental tests to probe anatomical hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use targeted experiments to test structural hypotheses (e.g. pouring quicksilver into a tied uterus to test for alternate passages: "The tuba did not stretch ... The uterus at TV stretched itself very much, by the quicksilver, and from thence I am convinced that it has no other passage than at X").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design simple mechanical/physical tests that reveal anatomical connectivity or function, and report setup and outcomes clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed anatomical description and inventory
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting dissections, enumerate organs, their number, placement, vascular supply and anomalies (example: full account of the monstrous double kitten listing stomachs, livers, veins, hearts, ribs, kidneys, diaphragms, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide thorough cataloguing of observed anatomy (presence/absence, duplications, relative sizes, vessel insertions) to allow assessment of the abnormality or normal form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include labelled figures and references to illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Support text with figures and explicit references to labelled parts (e.g. "as at K, pi. 5, fig. 6"; figs. 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 used to show organs and microscopic animals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide drawings/plates with labels and reference them in the narrative so visual evidence accompanies and clarifies the verbal description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report negative findings and observational limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Record absences and uncertain results plainly (e.g. "I could not find any body larger than a blood globule"; "I could not be positive").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State negative observations and uncertainty explicitly so others know what was searched for and not found; acknowledge limits of detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious interpretation; avoid overclaiming
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish observed entities from metaphysical or categorical claims (e.g. rejecting the claim that "worms in men's seed are children" and noting 'it is no less improper to say that the worms in men's seed are children, though children come from them').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret observations conservatively, avoid conflating analogous stages or using poetic/metaphorical language as literal explanation; state hypotheses separately from observed facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record temporal relations and contextual causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Document timing of events and contextual triggers (e.g. fits recurring on specific days or after fright; noting pregnancy and time after coitus when searching for seed), and relate them to observed outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include precise timings (days/hours) and relevant contextual events (trauma, fright, battle, delivery) to support causal inferences and to allow replication.
